Never-Sold: "There are no jails in Black Marsh. When a person does a wrong, they pay it in work, in nushmeekos. A nushmeeko is one month of work that nobody thanks you for, and once it is worked off nobody mentions it again. In the south that has gone bad. Whoever holds the estate or the landing does the reckoning, and he writes food, breakage and sickness onto the months until they never end. A person can be born owing and die owing. I was born owing, and I got out. That is why I do what I do."

result:
Rows-For-Another: "I holed a Tulm-Varo boat eleven years ago, and the Owing for it, the work I must do to pay, is not ended yet. The tree my tribe is hatched under is the Hist, and I have not stood under mine in all that time. Look at my arms. My colour is still mine, but every morning I look for the day it fades, and I think of walking home grey, with my own kin asking whose child I am. Three things hold me. The keeper, Hulm-Tei, stands at the doorway of the big house on the farm by the cattle and carries the key to the count-box inside, where my leaf lies, the page that says what I owe. His word is the second: by custom he may take the first price and close an Owing for good, and he has refused it. The third is Brings-Them-Back. He fetches runaways on this channel for a head-price, and he stands where it runs on north of this bank. He knows the way to my tree, so if I run while he lives, I can never go home. Each way out has its cost, as far as I know it. Lift my leaf from the box and my Owing goes with it. What that costs the keeper I cannot say. Ask for his word and you must move him, and he will tell you every line on my leaf is true: four months, then my food, then a fever. He is right. It has outgrown me. The channel costs most: buy the fetcher and he looks away, yet still knows my tree; kill him and I may go home, with a man dead for my sake. That is why I want my Owing closed, not fled. When the channel is clear, because he is dead or has agreed to look away, come and tell me."
